newsitem.title: UK: Glaxo H1 profits seen flat to lower.
newsitem.headline: Glaxo H1 profits seen flat to lower.

text.p: Glaxo Wellcome Plc is expected to report flat to slightly lower first half profits on July 31, restrained both by the strong pound and early erosion of its former best-selling product Zantac.
Analysts' forecasts are for pre-tax profit of between 1.480 and 1.550 billion stg, compared with 1.551 a year earlier.

Glaxo, the world's second-biggest drug company in terms of prescription drug sales, is now a quarter of the way through its promised two lean years of earnings and sales growth as it adjusts to the loss of patent on anti-ulcerant Zantac. Management has held out the prospect of strong renewed growth from 1999.

Zantac, which propelled Glaxo into the big time as the world's top-selling drug for 11 years in succession, lost its U.S. patent on Friday, with the first real impact therefore only to be felt in the second half.
However, many of the concerns about Glaxo's prospects following the patent expiry seem to have evaporated amid a rush of positive analyst comment in recent weeks.
Glaxo shares have soared by up to 50 percent this year, reaching a high of 1420 pence last week before succumbing to profit-taking. They were trading at 1334-1/2 pence around midday on Friday.

Analysts at Credit Suisse First Boston said earlier this month that Glaxo "is enjoying a renaissance as its management is convincingly persuading the market to overlook the imminent expiry of Zantac and focus on growing products that are replenishing the strong existing franchises and the new drugs that represent exciting high-growth opportunities."
And JP Morgan analyst Mark Becker issued a strong buy note on the stock in early July, predicting a re-rating of Glaxo shares in 1998.

Albert E Sharp analyst Vicky Wong said the share price had been performing strongly in recent weeks, approaching the ratings of U.S. drug companies at one point. "Everybody has been buying into the post-year 2000 growth," said Wong.
Wong said she expected Glaxo to reinforce its upbeat view of its prospects and drug portfolio.
Despite short-term problems Wong said Glaxo had a much more impressive portfolio of new products than British rivals SmithKline Beecham Plc or Zeneca Group Plc.

Analysts pointed to two potential blockbusters in the development pipeline, Lamivudine for hepatitis and Romozin for diabetes. There was also optimism about the group's strong AIDs franchise and the extension of asthma drug Serevent to cover conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a rapid deterioration in lung function affecting around one-fifth of all smokers.
